titleStmt.title: Memorandum From Michael V. Forrestal of the National Security Council Staff to President Kennedy

div.head: 477. Memorandum From Michael V. Forrestal of the National Security Council Staff to President Kennedy
div.p: A meeting is scheduled for 11 a.m. tomorrow morning for a discussion of planning with respect to the situation in Laos. Secretary Rusk, Secretary McNamara, Governor Harriman, Mr. Hilsman, Mr. McCone and General McKee (Acting Chairman of Joint Chiefs) are expected.

The purpose of the meeting is to get your reactions to the final version of a paper which you may already have read. It was included in your week end reading. The final version is attached (Tab A) and has been cleared by State, Defense and the J.C.S. It has been changed only in minor respects. Estimates of the time it would take for each phase to be completed have been removed, since it did not appear to be realistic to make such forecasts. There also has been a slight change in the objective of Phase 3. Instead of being designed to achieve only a “hard partition”
through a Geneva conference, it is now recognized that we would probably be satisfied if we had an enforceable cease-fire along a satisfactory line without necessarily having formal international sanction for it.

Unfortunately the major problem which has plagued us all along remains in this paper, i.e. the division between State and the military on the nature of the ultimate U.S. reaction. State believes that in order to convince North Vietnam and the ChiComs of the seriousness of U.S. intentions in Laos without running the danger of a rapid escalation, it is essential that some U.S. ground forces, if only of a token nature, be introduced into Laos before an air or ground attack upon North Vietnam.

Defense and the JCS maintain their position that no U.S. forces should be introduced into Laos except in connection with a simultaneous operation against North Vietnam. The military fear that unless our action and our objectives are clearly designed to eliminate the heart of the threat in Hanoi, to introduce troops into Laos would risk long term commitment of U.S. personnel under the most adverse military circumstances.
This disagreement is spelled out on pages 13 and 14 of the Memorandum.

A special national intelligence estimate (SNIE 58–63 Tab B)/3/has been prepared and will be presented to you by Mr. McCone. Although the estimate concludes that Phases 1 and 2 would achieve the desired result of bringing about negotiations with Communists on a cease-fire; it does not give a confident estimate of Communist reactions to Phase 3.

In light of the fact that the situation in Laos continues to deteriorate and in light of the disagreement between State and the military (which has nevertheless greatly narrowed). I suggest that you consider taking the following actions: (1)
Indicate your approval of the steps outlined in Phases 1 and 2 (pages 3–7) and direct that those steps be implemented which do not violate the sovereignty of North Vietnam. You will be out of the country while some of these are being put in motion. (2)
Ask for further refinement and study of the remainder of Phase 2 and Phase 3. You could indicate you would like another meeting when you return from Europe. (3)
Suggest that in the course of this review and refinement, the military consider the use of U.S. Army special forces in Laos in Phase 2 or early in Phase 3. As you know, these forces have been created by the Army for guerrilla-type activity over difficult terrain. Introducing some units of the Army special forces into Laos as fighters might be sufficiently overt to make the signal to the North Vietnamese which the State
Department desires. They would, however, not represent a massive commitment of American personnel which the Pentagon fears, and they could, presumably, be withdrawn if necessary.
You may wish to do some very gentle prodding to ease the military out of their muscle-bound, all-or-nothing view of Southeast Asia.
A current estimate of the situation in Laos is attached as Tab C.

note.p: Source: Kennedy Library, President’s Office Files, Countries, Laos Security, Laos Planning Material, 6/18/63. Top Secret.
Tab B, entitled “Communist Reactions to US Actions Taken With Regard to Laos,” is not printed. (Kennedy Library, National Security Files, Countries Series, Laos: General, 6/16/63–6/30/63).
Not found, unless Forrestal is referring to the introduction to the phases paper,
